question.text: A portfolio manager at Saraswati Private Equity Fund is pitching an LP on a classic 'pure-play private equity' strategy vs a venture capital strategy. Per NISM Chapter 2.3.2, which statement BEST captures the CONVENTIONAL distinction?

answer.text: Venture capital is always illegal in India without RBI approval, while PE is SEBI-regulated.
PE invests only in listed companies, while VC invests only in unlisted companies.

Pure-play PE provides growth capital to later-stage unlisted companies with established business models and track records, while venture capital finances early-stage, unproven businesses with higher mortality risk.
PE and VC are identical in strategy; the only difference is the size of the cheque.

explanation.text: The Logic: Per Chapter 2.3.2, the term 'private equity' is 'predominantly used to denote investment in companies with established business model and track record (known as later stage companies)' and the pure-play PE model 'revolves around providing growth capital to later stage unlisted companies'. Chapter 2.3.1 contrasts this with VC which targets 'infant companies... yet to grow or evolve completely' with 'high mortality rate'. The Trap: Option A is false — VC is SEBI-regulated as a Cat I AIF sub-category. Option C is false — PE also makes private (unlisted) investments predominantly, and can also take positions in listed companies per Ch 2.3.2. Option D ignores the stage-of-investee distinction which is the whole point. Cross-Exam Context: XIX-A tests the Cat I sub-classification (VCF vs SSF vs Infra) for distribution. XIX-C as the manager exam tests the economic logic. Manager's Pro-Tip: Your fund's 'stage' positioning in the PPM drives everything — LP base, fee schedule, benchmark, DPI expectation. Late-stage PE LPs expect 2.0-2.5x TVPI and DPI by year 5; early-stage VC LPs expect 3x+ TVPI but accept DPI only by year 8-10. Don't blur the pitch.
